title: Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis
subject: Paediatrics
summary: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is an immune-mediated glomerular injury following a group A streptococcal infection. It typically presents as acute nephritic syndrome with haematuria, hypertension, and fluid overload. Management is largely supportive, focusing on strict fluid management and blood pressure control.

sections.p: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is an immune-complex-mediated inflammation of the renal glomeruli occurring after pharyngeal or cutaneous infection with nephritogenic strains of Streptococcus pyogenes.
b: Requires evidence of recent streptococcal infection plus nephritic syndrome.
Nephritic syndrome triad: macroscopic haematuria, hypertension, and periorbital oedema.
Characterised by hypocomplementaemia (depressed serum C3) returning to normal within 8 weeks.

sections.p: There is no formal anatomical staging system; clinical severity is staged by the presence of end-organ compromise caused by volume overload and elevated blood pressure.
b: Mild: Microscopic or tea-coloured haematuria, mild facial puffiness, normal blood pressure, preserved urine output.
Moderate: Frank cola-coloured urine, obvious periorbital and peripheral oedema, stage 1 hypertension, mild oliguria.
Severe: Stage 2 hypertension, acute kidney injury, hypertensive encephalopathy (seizures, altered mental state), or acute pulmonary oedema.

sections.p: The primary cause is an abnormal immune response following a group A beta-haemolytic streptococcal infection.
b: Pharyngitis-associated PSGN: Follows throat infection after a latent period of 1 to 3 weeks.
Pyoderma-associated PSGN: Follows impetigo or infected scabies lesions after a latent period of 3 to 6 weeks.
Co-existent conditions in tropical settings: Scabies infestation and tropical ulcers often trigger the initiating streptococcal pyoderma.
Other post-infectious mimics: Glomerulonephritis associated with infective endocarditis, shunt nephritis, quartan malaria, or severe hepatitis B.

sections.p: Children aged 5 to 12 years present acutely with sudden facial swelling, reduced urine volume, and discoloured urine.
b: History of sore throat 1 to 3 weeks prior, or skin sores 3 to 6 weeks prior.
Smoky, tea-coloured, or cola-coloured urine due to glomerular bleeding.
Periorbital oedema, especially marked in the early morning upon waking.
Oliguria with low daily urine volumes.
Headache, nausea, vomiting, or seizures resulting from severe acute hypertension.
Breathlessness, orthopnoea, and tachypnoea indicating circulatory congestion and fluid overload.

sections.p: In resource-constrained settings lacking complement assays or streptococcal serology, clinical diagnosis relies on the nephritic triad following impetigo or pharyngitis with recovery after fluid management.

t.b: Confirms active glomerular bleeding; shows haematuria, mild-to-moderate proteinuria, and dysmorphic red blood cells with red cell casts.
Determines immune complex pathway activation; low C3 with normal C4 strongly supports PSGN and resolves in 6 to 8 weeks.
Confirms prior streptococcal infection; ASO rises after pharyngitis, while anti-DNase B is far more sensitive for prior skin infections.
Quantifies severity of acute kidney injury and determines urgency of fluid restriction and potential dialysis need.
Detects life-threatening hyperkalaemia resulting from severe oliguria or acute renal failure.
Evaluates suspected pulmonary oedema, cardiomegaly, or pleural effusions in severe fluid overload; guided clinically if unavailable.

sections.p: Life-threatening complications arise rapidly from sudden hypertension and intravascular fluid expansion.
b: Hypertensive encephalopathy: Severe headache, visual disturbances, vomiting, altered consciousness, and generalised seizures.
Acute pulmonary oedema: Severe tachypnoea, hypoxia, grunting, gallop rhythm, and widespread fine pulmonary crackles.
Hyperkalaemia: Peaked T waves, widening QRS complexes, and lethal cardiac arrhythmias secondary to anuria.
Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis: Rapid deterioration of renal function over days to weeks, requiring urgent specialist referral.

sections.p: Management focuses on eliminating persistent streptococcal carriage, correcting severe circulatory overload, and maintaining tight control of blood pressure.
b: Bed rest and daily weighing: Daily weight and strict intake-output charts provide the best guide to fluid status.
Fluid restriction: Total volume limited to insensible losses plus previous 24-hour urine output during oliguric phases.
Dietary sodium restriction: Strict restriction of salt intake to relieve volume expansion and hypertension.
Loop diuretics: Oral or intravenous furosemide is first-line to induce diuresis, offload fluid, and reduce blood pressure.
Antihypertensive agents: Calcium channel blockers (such as amlodipine or nifedipine) or hydralazine are used if hypertension persists despite diuresis.
Antihypertensives to avoid acutely: ACE inhibitors are avoided in the acute phase due to hyperkalaemia risk and worsening renal perfusion.
Antibiotic therapy: Oral penicillin V or erythromycin eradicates lingering nephritogenic strains and stops spread to close contacts; does not reverse established nephritis.
Immunosuppressants: Corticosteroids are not routinely indicated, though reserved for atypical presentations or biopsy-proven crescentic disease.

sections.p: Clinical resolution typically follows a predictable timeline, with long-term prognosis remaining excellent in over 95 percent of children.
b: Diuresis usually commences within 7 to 10 days, followed by blood pressure normalisation.
C3 complement levels must be rechecked at 8 to 12 weeks; failure to normalise requires renal biopsy.
Microscopic haematuria may persist harmlessly for up to 1 to 2 years.
Treat primary streptococcal throat and skin infections promptly to limit community spread.
Mass community treatment of scabies and pyoderma prevents endemic clusters in low-resource environments.

sections.p: Distinguishing PSGN from other paediatric causes of oedema and haematuria prevents inappropriate therapy.
b: Nephrotic syndrome: Marked by heavy proteinuria and severe generalised oedema; lacks gross haematuria, hypertension, and low C3.
IgA nephropathy: Recurrent gross haematuria occurring during or within 1 to 2 days of mucosal infection (synpharyngitic), with normal C3.
Lupus nephritis: Nephritic or nephrotic features accompanied by low C3 and low C4, positive antinuclear antibodies, and systemic signs.
Malaria nephropathy: Blackwater fever or quartan malarial glomerulopathy in endemic areas; confirmed via blood film and thick smear.
Post-infective endocarditis nephritis: Persistent fever, cardiac murmurs, and low complements, requiring prolonged bactericidal antibiotics.

sections.p: Several bedside and laboratory investigations can produce misleading results if interpreted without clinical context.
b: ASO titres in skin infections: Often falsely negative or low following pyoderma; anti-DNase B testing is required instead.
Early antibiotic use: Prompt antibiotic therapy given for the initial sore throat can blunt the expected rise in streptococcal serology.
Urine dipstick red colour: Coca-cola urine may represent myoglobinuria or haemoglobinuria without intact erythrocytes unless verified by microscopy.
Transient C3 depression: Other conditions, like membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, cause hypocomplementaemia that persists beyond 8 to 12 weeks.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset of severe headache, vomiting, or seizures
Severe shortness of breath, orthopnoea, or coughing pink frothy sputum
Complete absence of urine output for 12 hours or longer
Drowsiness, confusion, or difficulty waking the child

faq.q: Why are ACE inhibitors avoided during the acute phase of PSGN?
faq.a: ACE inhibitors reduce glomerular filtration pressure and hinder potassium excretion, increasing the risk of severe hyperkalaemia and worsening acute kidney injury in an already oliguric child.

faq.q: Does treating a streptococcal sore throat prevent PSGN?
faq.a: Unlike rheumatic fever, early antibiotic treatment of streptococcal pharyngitis or impetigo does not reliably prevent the subsequent development of PSGN, though it prevents spread to contacts.

faq.q: How long does it take for the urine colour and laboratory tests to normalise?
faq.a: Gross cola-coloured haematuria clears within days to weeks. Serum C3 levels normalise within 8 weeks, while microscopic haematuria can take up to 1 to 2 years to fully disappear.

exam: A 7-year-old child presents with tea-coloured urine and eyelid swelling 2 weeks after a sore throat. What are the key components of the initial bedside assessment? — Check blood pressure against paediatric percentiles, assess for signs of fluid overload (gallop rhythm, fine pulmonary crackles, hepatomegaly), and perform a urine dipstick for protein and blood.

Why might an ASO titre be entirely normal in a child with biopsy-confirmed PSGN following infected scabies lesions? — Anti-streptolysin O rises poorly after cutaneous streptococcal infections because skin lipids inactivate streptolysin O; an anti-DNase B or antihyaluronidase titre is the preferred test.

A patient with PSGN and severe hypertension develops a generalised tonic-clonic seizure. What is the immediate pathophysiological cause and management priority? — Hypertensive encephalopathy secondary to fluid overload; manage with airway protection, prompt administration of an intravenous loop diuretic like furosemide, and a parenteral antihypertensive.

How does the timing of haematuria help distinguish IgA nephropathy from PSGN? — IgA nephropathy features synpharyngitic haematuria occurring concurrently or within 1 to 2 days of infection, whereas PSGN follows a latent period of 1 to 3 weeks post-pharyngitis or 3 to 6 weeks post-pyoderma.

What finding at 8 to 12 weeks of follow-up would mandate a percutaneous renal biopsy? — Persistent hypocomplementaemia (low serum C3), persistent heavy nephrotic-range proteinuria, or progressive renal failure, suggesting alternative conditions like membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.

What is the rationale for prescribing penicillin to a child diagnosed with acute PSGN when the disease is immune-mediated? — Penicillin does not alter the course or hasten resolution of the active glomerular disease; it is given solely to eradicate residual carriage of nephritogenic streptococci and prevent transmission to contacts.

Why are loop diuretics preferred over standard first-line adult antihypertensives in managing PSGN hypertension? — Hypertension in PSGN is driven primarily by intravascular sodium and water retention rather than systemic vasoconstriction; loop diuretics offload volume, directly reversing the underlying mechanism.
